title: Hospitals of the Islamic Golden Age
summary: How great hospitals in cities such as Baghdad, Damascus, and Cairo gave free care, sorted patients into wards, trained doctors, and shaped the hospitals we use today.
poll: Hospitals from a thousand years ago have nothing to teach us today.

versions.title: Great Hospitals Long Ago
versions.text:
Long ago, there were great hospitals. It was more than a thousand years ago. Baghdad had one. So did more big towns.

Who could go? All the sick! Rich or poor? It was free. Each patient got a bed. Each got food. Each got clean clothes. It was a kind place.

Each sickness had its own ward. Bad eyes had one. Fevers had one. Medicine was mixed there, too.

Doctors taught there. Young men came to learn. They watched and read. They learned a lot. In Baghdad, each one had to pass a test.

Al-Razi was a great doctor. A tale says he hung meat round the town. Where did it rot last? That spot had the best air. So the hospital was built there! He wrote on two ills with spots, too.

Ibn Sina was great, too. He wrote a huge book on how to heal. In Europe, it was used for a long time.

One in Cairo gave the sick some cash. They got it as they left. Then they could rest at home.

We still do lots of these things. Think of that next time you are sick!

versions.text:

Ibn Sina was another great physician. He wrote a giant book about medicine, and doctors in Europe studied it for hundreds of years.

One huge hospital in Cairo was generous in a new way. It gave some patients money as they left, so they could rest at home before going back to work.

Many of these ideas are still used in hospitals today.

versions.title: Hospitals of the Islamic Golden Age
versions.text:
More than a thousand years ago, major cities throughout the Islamic world constructed impressive hospitals, which people called bimaristans, a Persian word meaning "place for the sick." Famous examples stood in Baghdad, Damascus, and Cairo, and some were spacious enough to accommodate hundreds of people simultaneously.

Anyone who was sick could seek assistance at a bimaristan, because it did not matter whether you were wealthy or impoverished, a man or a woman, and the treatment was entirely free. Each patient received a bed, nourishing meals, and clean clothing.

Rather than remaining together in one crowded room, the sick were separated, and each category of disease had its own ward, so people with eye conditions stayed in one section while people with fevers stayed in another. Each hospital also contained a pharmacy, where trained workers carefully prepared medicines from herbs, minerals, and other natural ingredients.

These hospitals were also significant institutions of learning. Young men observed each physician examine patients and diagnose their illnesses, and they studied manuscripts in the hospital library. In Baghdad, in the year 931, a new regulation required doctors to pass an official exam before they were permitted to practice medicine, a rule that was reportedly introduced after a patient died because of a doctor's error.

Al-Razi was a celebrated physician in Baghdad. According to a well-known story, he suspended pieces of meat in different neighborhoods and selected the location where the meat decayed most slowly, since he believed the air there was cleanest and therefore healthiest for a hospital. Al-Razi also wrote about two diseases that cause spots, smallpox and measles, and he meticulously described the symptoms that enable doctors to distinguish one from the other.

Ibn Sina, another brilliant physician, composed an enormous book called The Canon of Medicine, which functioned like a medical encyclopedia, and European doctors studied it for hundreds of years.

One enormous hospital in Cairo was generous in an unusual way, because it gave some patients money as they departed, so they could recuperate at home before returning to work.

Many of these innovations, from separate wards to professional examinations, are still used in hospitals today.

versions.title: Hospitals of the Islamic Golden Age
versions.text:
More than a thousand years ago, major cities throughout the Islamic world constructed impressive hospitals, which people called bimaristans, a Persian word meaning "place for the sick." Celebrated examples stood in Baghdad, Damascus, and Cairo, and some were sufficiently spacious to accommodate hundreds of people simultaneously.

Anyone who was sick could seek assistance at a bimaristan, because it did not matter whether you were wealthy or impoverished, a man or a woman, and the treatment was entirely free of charge. Each patient received a bed, nourishing meals, and clean clothing.

Rather than remaining together in one crowded room, the sick were separated, and each category of disease had its own ward, so people with eye conditions stayed in one section while people with fevers occupied another. Each hospital also contained a pharmacy, where trained workers meticulously prepared medicines from herbs, minerals, and other natural ingredients according to written formulas.

These hospitals were also significant institutions of learning, where young men observed each physician examine patients and diagnose their illnesses, and where they studied manuscripts in the hospital library. In Baghdad, in the year 931, a new regulation required doctors to pass an official exam before they were permitted to practice medicine independently, a regulation that was reportedly introduced after a patient died as a consequence of a physician's error.

Al-Razi was a distinguished physician in Baghdad. According to a well-known story, he suspended pieces of meat in different neighborhoods and selected the location where the meat decayed most slowly, since he reasoned that the air there was cleanest and therefore healthiest for a hospital. Al-Razi also wrote about two diseases that cause spots, smallpox and measles, and he meticulously described the symptoms that enable doctors to distinguish one from the other.

Ibn Sina, another brilliant physician, composed an enormous book called The Canon of Medicine, which functioned like a comprehensive medical encyclopedia, and European doctors studied it for hundreds of years.

One enormous hospital in Cairo was generous in an unusual way, because it provided some patients with money as they departed, so they could recuperate at home before returning to their employment.

Many of these innovations, from specialized wards to professional examinations, are still used in hospitals today, which is why historians regard the bimaristans as important ancestors of the modern hospital.

keyWords.example: The doctor listened to my heart.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: Great hospitals of long ago and how they helped the sick
How to become a doctor today
The life of one sick child in Cairo
How to cook meat so it stays fresh
questions.why: The article tells about great hospitals built more than a thousand years ago and the ways they cared for sick people.

wrong.B: The article tells how doctors trained long ago, not how to become one today.
wrong.C: The article is not about one child.
wrong.D: Meat is part of a story about choosing a place, not about cooking.

questions.stem: Who could get care at these hospitals?
options: Only rich people
Only men
Only doctors and their families
Anyone who was sick, rich or poor
questions.why: The article says all the sick could go, rich or poor, and the care was free.

wrong.A: The article says it did not matter if you were rich or poor.
wrong.B: The article does not say only men could go.
wrong.C: The hospitals were for all the sick, not just doctors.

questions.stem: What did a doctor in Baghdad have to do before working?
options: Build a hospital
Pass a test
Hang meat in the town
Write a book
questions.why: The article says that in Baghdad a doctor had to pass a test first.

wrong.A: Doctors did not have to build hospitals.
wrong.C: Hanging meat is from the story about Al-Razi, not a rule for all doctors.
wrong.D: Some doctors wrote books, but it was not a rule.

questions.stem: What does the word ward mean in this article?
options: A test for a new doctor
A huge book about healing
A part of a hospital for one kind of sickness
A gift of money for a patient
questions.why: The article says each sickness had its own ward, such as one for bad eyes and one for fevers.

wrong.A: The test is something doctors had to pass, not a ward.
wrong.B: The huge book was written by Ibn Sina.
wrong.D: Money was given in Cairo, but that is not a ward.

questions.stem: Why was a hospital built where the meat went bad last?
options: The air there was the best.
The town had the most food there.
It was close to the river.
It was where Al-Razi lived.
questions.why: The article says the spot where the meat went bad last had the best, cleanest air, so the hospital was built there.

wrong.B: The article does not talk about food in that part of town.
wrong.C: No river is named in the article.
wrong.D: The article does not say where Al-Razi lived.

questions.stem: Why do you think the hospital in Cairo gave some patients money when they left?
options: So they could buy more medicine at the market
So they would come back to work at the hospital
So they could rest at home before working
So they could pay the doctors next time
questions.why: The article says the money meant they could rest at home. Without it, they might have had to go back to work while still weak.

wrong.A: The article does not say the money was for medicine.
wrong.B: The patients were not hospital workers.
wrong.D: The care was free, so they did not have to pay the doctors.

questions.stem: Why did each sickness probably have its own ward?
options: So the hospital could save money
So each group could get the right care
So the doctors could sleep there
So patients could not see their families
questions.why: Putting people with the same sickness together, like those with bad eyes, makes it easier to give them the care they need.

wrong.A: The article does not link wards with saving money.
wrong.C: The wards were for patients, not for doctors to sleep.
wrong.D: The article never says families were kept away.

questions.stem: Why does the author end by saying we still use many of these ideas?
options: To tell readers to visit Baghdad
To show that the hospitals were very small
To explain how to mix medicine
To show that these old hospitals still matter
questions.why: The last line connects the old hospitals to hospitals today, showing why they are still important.

wrong.A: The author does not ask readers to travel.
wrong.B: The article says some hospitals were huge.
wrong.C: The last line does not explain how to mix medicine.

wrong.C: The book is about medicine, not hospital rules.
wrong.D: Ibn Sina wrote the book; it is not a story about Al-Razi.

questions.stem: Why does the article call the hospitals institutions of learning?
options: They were built next to universities.
Patients had to pass exams before entering.
Students watched physicians diagnose patients and studied there.
Every patient was taught to read.
questions.why: The article says young men observed physicians examine and diagnose patients and studied manuscripts in the hospital library.

wrong.A: The article does not mention universities nearby.
wrong.B: Doctors, not patients, had to pass exams.
wrong.D: The article does not say patients were taught to read.

questions.stem: What was one result of Al-Razi's description of smallpox and measles?
options: Both diseases disappeared from Baghdad.
Doctors could tell the two diseases apart by their symptoms.
Hospitals stopped accepting patients with spots.
Ibn Sina copied it into a poem.
questions.why: The article says he described the symptoms that help doctors distinguish one disease from the other.

wrong.A: The article does not say the diseases disappeared.
wrong.C: The article says anyone who was sick could seek help.
wrong.D: The article does not connect Ibn Sina with a poem.

questions.stem: What does the meat story suggest about Al-Razi's way of thinking?
options: He believed cooks should run hospitals.
He preferred to choose places at random.
He thought meat could cure disease.
He tested his ideas by careful observation.
questions.why: Instead of guessing, he compared how fast meat decayed in different places and used that evidence to choose a healthy site.

wrong.A: The story is about choosing clean air, not about cooks.
wrong.B: He compared places carefully, which is the opposite of random.
wrong.C: The meat was a test of the air, not a treatment.

questions.stem: According to the article, what did the regulation of 931 require?
options: Doctors had to pass an exam before practicing.
Every city had to build a bimaristan.
Patients had to pay for their medicine.
Students had to study The Canon of Medicine.
questions.why: The article states that in Baghdad in 931 a new regulation required doctors to pass an exam before practicing.

wrong.B: The rule was about doctors, not about building hospitals.
wrong.C: Treatment was free, and the rule did not concern payment.
wrong.D: The article does not link this rule to Ibn Sina's book.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention that the Cairo hospital gave patients money as they departed?
options: To show that the hospital was very wealthy
To explain how doctors were paid
To show care for patients' full recovery
To compare Cairo with Damascus
questions.why: The money let patients recuperate at home before returning to work, which shows concern for their complete recovery.

wrong.A: The point is the patients' recovery, not the hospital's wealth.
wrong.B: The money went to patients, not doctors.
wrong.D: No comparison with Damascus is made in that paragraph.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says that hospitals from a thousand years ago have nothing to teach us today. Do you agree or disagree? Support your answer with at least two examples from the article.
checklist: I stated a clear opinion about the poll.
I supported it with at least two accurate examples from the article.
I used the words institution and diagnose or symptom correctly.
